narrative_md:
**HMRC says the UK tax gap is 4.8% — one of the lowest in the world. Tax Justice UK says the real hole is closer to three times that.**

HMRC's 2024 Measuring Tax Gaps publication put the 2022-23 gap at £39.8 billion, or 4.8% of theoretical liabilities. Campaigners and some academics say the official methodology systematically under-captures offshore evasion, profit shifting and the long tail of disguised remuneration. The dispute matters because every £1bn of closed gap is a £1bn that does not need to come from working taxpayers.

**HMRC's official number is £39.8 billion.** It is published every June in the Measuring Tax Gaps series and has declined from 7.5% of theoretical liability in 2005-06 to 4.8% in 2022-23. On paper, this makes the UK one of the best-performing tax administrations in the OECD. The largest single slice is small-business non-compliance (roughly 60% of the total), followed by evasion, criminal attacks and avoidance. Large corporates and wealthy individuals, according to HMRC, contribute only a small share.

Tax Justice UK and the Tax Justice Network challenge that framing. Their 2023-24 estimate put the true annual gap between £90bn and £120bn — two to three times HMRC's figure — by including offshore wealth invisible to UK registers, transfer-pricing abuse by multinationals routing profits through low-tax jurisdictions, and the residual effect of the Loan Charge cohort who have moved their arrangements offshore after 2019 settlement terms. The Common Reporting Standard (CRS) data-share, fully operational since 2018, identified roughly £850m of previously undeclared offshore income in its first four years — a fraction of what academics working from Switzerland and Cayman Islands deposit totals would predict.

The Loan Charge itself is the most toxic thread. Introduced by the 2017 Finance Act and applied retrospectively to disguised-remuneration schemes dating back to 1999, it created tax demands up to 20 years after the fact for around 50,000 contractors — many of them IT and health-sector workers who had been advised by their own accountants that the schemes were legal. By 2024 the APPG on the Loan Charge had linked ten suicides to the policy. The Morse Review in 2019 narrowed its scope. The 2024 Budget announced a fresh independent review under James Murray, reporting late 2025.

Offshore evasion is the hardest piece to measure because HMRC's methodology relies on observable data — tax returns, VAT records, random audits. Wealth parked in offshore trusts, layered behind nominee directors, simply does not appear in those datasets. The 2021 Pandora Papers leak identified hundreds of UK-linked offshore structures; HMRC's follow-up was published in 2024 and recovered roughly £50m in additional assessments — again, a fraction of what academic estimates of hidden UK offshore wealth (Zucman: £300bn+) would imply.

The R&D tax-credit fraud scandal is the mirror image. Here the gap is admitted: HMRC raised its R&D error-and-fraud estimate from 3.6% in 2020-21 to 16.7% (SME scheme) in 2022-23, implying £1.1bn of the £7bn paid out was incorrect. The April 2024 merger of the SME and RDEC schemes and the 2025 enhanced-support scheme for loss-making R&D-intensive SMEs are the policy response, alongside a tripled compliance team at HMRC Croydon.

The political economy is the reason this story keeps running. Every Chancellor from Hammond to Reeves has announced a crackdown on evasion in Budget Red Books; every successor inherits a still-uncollected gap. Reeves's October 2024 Budget pledged £555m of additional HMRC funding to raise £6.5bn by 2029-30 — a ratio of 12-to-1. If the Tax Justice number is closer to truth, the policy response is still roughly one order of magnitude too small.
